title: Presentation and disclosure: classification and aggregation
summary: How presentation and disclosure communicate information, classification of assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses, offsetting, profit or loss, and aggregation.

chunks.heading: Presentation and disclosure as communication tools
chunks.explanation_md:
An entity communicates information about its assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses by **presenting and disclosing** it in its statements. Effective communication makes information **more relevant**, contributes to a **faithful representation**, and improves **understandability and comparability**. It requires:

(a) focusing on **presentation and disclosure objectives and principles**, rather than on rules;
(b) **classifying** information so that **similar items are grouped and dissimilar items separated**; and
(c) **aggregating** information so that it is not obscured by **unnecessary detail or excessive aggregation**.

**Cost** constrains these decisions too: benefits must justify costs.

**Objectives and principles in Standards.** A balance is needed between (a) giving entities the **flexibility** to give relevant, faithful information, and (b) requiring information that is **comparable**, from period to period and across entities. Including **objectives** in Standards helps entities identify useful information and decide how to communicate it. Two principles support effective communication: (a) **entity-specific information** is more useful than **standardised descriptions** (boilerplate); and (b) **duplication** of information in different parts of the statements is usually unnecessary and can make them **less understandable**.
chunks.exam_line: Effective communication needs objectives and principles over rules, classification (group similar, separate dissimilar) and balanced aggregation. Entity-specific information beats boilerplate; avoid duplication.

chunks.heading: Classification and offsetting
chunks.explanation_md:
**Classification** is the sorting of assets, liabilities, equity, income or expenses on the basis of **shared characteristics** for presentation and disclosure. Characteristics include, but are not limited to: the **nature** of the item, its **role (function)** within the business activities, and **how it is measured**.

Classifying **dissimilar items together** can obscure relevant information, reduce understandability and comparability, and may not be a faithful representation.

**Assets and liabilities.** Classification is applied to the selected unit of account, but it may be appropriate to **separate an asset or liability into components with different characteristics** and classify them separately, for example into **current and non-current** components.

**Offsetting.** Offsetting occurs when an entity recognises and measures an asset and a liability as **separate units of account** but groups them into **a single net amount** in the statement of financial position. It classifies dissimilar items together and is **generally not appropriate**. It differs from treating a set of rights and obligations as one unit of account.

**Equity.** It may be necessary to classify equity claims separately if they have **different characteristics**, and components separately if subject to particular **legal, regulatory or other requirements**, for example reserves that are **distributable**.

key_terms.meaning: The sorting of assets, liabilities, equity, income or expenses on the basis of shared characteristics for presentation and disclosure.
Grouping an asset and a liability that are recognised and measured as separate units of account into a single net amount in the statement of financial position.

chunks.heading: Classification of income and expenses: profit or loss and other comprehensive income
chunks.explanation_md:
Classification applies to income and expenses from the selected unit of account, or to **components** with different characteristics identified separately. For example, a change in the current value of an asset can include **value changes and accrual of interest**, and it would be appropriate to classify them separately if that helps users.

**Profit or loss and other comprehensive income.** Income and expenses are classified and included either in the **statement of profit or loss** or, outside it, in **other comprehensive income**.

- The statement of profit or loss is the **primary source of information about financial performance**. Its **total for profit or loss** is a highly summarised depiction many users use as a starting point or main indicator. But understanding performance needs an analysis of **all** recognised income and expenses, including those in other comprehensive income, and other information in the statements.
- Because of this, **in principle all income and expenses are included in profit or loss**. In **exceptional circumstances** the Board may decide in a Standard that income or expenses from a **change in the current value** of an asset or liability go in other comprehensive income, when that would make profit or loss **more relevant or more faithful**.
- Income and expenses that arise on a **historical cost basis** are included in profit or loss. This also holds when they are identified as a component of a change in current value. For example, if a financial asset is at current value and **interest income** is identified separately, that interest is in profit or loss.
- In principle, amounts in other comprehensive income are **reclassified** into profit or loss in a future period when that makes profit or loss more relevant or faithful. But if there is no clear basis for identifying the period or amount, the Board may decide in a Standard that they are **not reclassified**.
chunks.exam_line: In principle all income and expenses go in profit or loss; in exceptional cases some go in other comprehensive income and are in principle reclassified later. Profit or loss is the primary source of performance information.

chunks.heading: Aggregation
chunks.explanation_md:
**Aggregation** is the adding together of assets, liabilities, equity, income or expenses that have **shared characteristics** and are in the **same classification**.

Aggregation makes information more useful by **summarising a large volume of detail**, but it **conceals some of that detail**. So a balance is needed so that relevant information is **not obscured by a large amount of insignificant detail** or by **excessive aggregation**.

Different levels of aggregation may be needed in different parts of the statements. For example, the statement of financial position and the statement(s) of financial performance usually give **summarised** information and the **notes** give the **more detailed** information.

chunks.exam_line: Aggregation summarises detail but hides some; balance insignificant detail against excessive aggregation. The statements summarise, the notes give detail.

questions.stem: Explain how income and expenses are classified between profit or loss and other comprehensive income.
questions.model_answer_md:
Income and expenses are classified and included either in the **statement of profit or loss** or in **other comprehensive income**.

The statement of profit or loss is the **primary source** of information about performance, and its total is a highly summarised depiction. Therefore **all income and expenses are in principle included in it**. In exceptional circumstances a Standard may place income or expenses from a change in the current value of an asset or liability in other comprehensive income, if that makes profit or loss more relevant or more faithful.

Income and expenses on a **historical cost basis** are included in profit or loss, including interest identified separately within a change in current value. Items in other comprehensive income are in principle **reclassified** into profit or loss in a later period when that gives more relevant or faithful information, unless there is no clear basis.

questions.stem: Discuss presentation and disclosure as communication tools, including classification, offsetting and aggregation.
questions.model_answer_md:
An entity communicates information by **presenting and disclosing** it in the statements. Effective communication makes information more relevant, supports faithful representation and improves understandability and comparability. It needs a focus on **objectives and principles rather than rules**, **classification** and **aggregation**. **Cost** constrains it.

**Objectives and principles.** A balance is needed between giving entities flexibility to provide relevant, faithful information and requiring comparable information across periods and entities. Objectives help entities identify useful information. Two principles: entity-specific information is more useful than standardised descriptions (boilerplate); and duplication is usually unnecessary and may reduce understandability.

**Classification.** Sorting on shared characteristics (nature, function, how measured). Classifying dissimilar items together obscures information. Items may be separated into components such as current and non-current, and equity claims and components with legal restrictions may be classified separately. **Offsetting** nets a recognised asset and liability and is generally not appropriate.

**Income and expenses.** Classified into profit or loss or other comprehensive income; profit or loss is the primary source, and all items are in principle in it.

**Aggregation.** Adding together items with shared characteristics in the same classification. It summarises detail but conceals some, so a balance is needed; the statements summarise and the notes give detail.

questions.stem: Explain the classification of equity and of assets and liabilities, and why dissimilar items should not be classified together.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Why not together.** Classifying dissimilar assets, liabilities, equity, income or expenses together can **obscure relevant information**, reduce understandability and comparability, and may not be a faithful representation.

**Assets and liabilities.** Classification is applied to the selected **unit of account**. It may be appropriate to separate an asset or liability into **components with different characteristics** and classify them separately, for example **current and non-current** components, when that makes the information more useful.

**Equity.** To give useful information it may be necessary to classify **equity claims separately** if they have different characteristics, and to classify **components of equity** separately if they are subject to legal, regulatory or other requirements. For example, where distributions are allowed only out of specified **distributable reserves**, separate presentation or disclosure of those reserves may be useful.

**Offsetting** an asset and a liability into a net amount classifies dissimilar items together and is generally not appropriate.
